I've now gathered extensive material from across the approved sources. Let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from what I could access.

## Matthew 26:26–50 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### v. 26 — "While they were eating, Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, 'Take and eat; this is My body.'"

- **Traditional Reading (Gill, Ellicott, Spurgeon, Enduring Word):** This occurred *during* the Passover meal. Jesus took one of the unleavened cakes, spoke a blessing over it (distinct from the initial grace at the meal's start), broke it, and distributed it. The words "this is My body" have been the centre of immense theological controversy. **Spurgeon** states plainly: "Christ could not have meant that the bread was his body, for his body was reclining by the table; but he intended that broken bread to represent his body which was about to be broken on the cross." He adds there is "no trace here of any altar or priest; there is nothing about the elevation or adoration of the host; there is no resemblance between the Lord's supper and the Romish mass." **Ellicott** likewise calls theories of transubstantiation and consubstantiation "alien to the mind of Christ" and notes that Jesus' language was "figurative boldness" — like "I am the door" (John 10:7). The disciples would understand that His body was "as truly given for them as that bread which He had broken was given to them." **Gill** emphasises that the bread is a sign and seal of Christ's body, not the body itself, and that the breaking signifies His sufferings. (Sources: biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm; preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon)

- **Reformed View (Ligonier):** The bread and wine are "sacramental signs" — there is a "spiritual relation, or sacramental union, between the sign and the thing signified." Christ is "really, but spiritually, present to the faith of believers" — not corporally in/with/under the elements. The Westminster Confession teaches that worthy receivers "inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ crucified." (learn.ligonier.org/articles/what-lords-supper)

- **Lutheran View (lcms.org, 1517.org):** Lutherans teach the *real bodily presence* of Christ "in, with, and under" the bread and wine (often called consubstantiation, though Lutherans themselves reject that term). Christ's body and blood are truly present and received by all communicants, not merely by faith. The bread remains bread and Christ's body is truly present. (learn.ligonier.org/guides/the-lords-supper — noting the Lutheran position contrast with Reformed)

- **Catholic View (newadvent.org, catholic.com):** The Church teaches *transubstantiation* — the entire substance of bread is converted into the substance of Christ's body, and the entire substance of wine into His blood, while the accidents (appearances) of bread and wine remain. The Catholic Encyclopedia states: "The words of Institution were at the same time the words of Transubstantiation." It argues that had Christ intended mere symbolism or coexistence, He would have said "this bread contains my body" rather than the simple identification "this is my body." (newadvent.org/cathen/05573a.htm; catholic.com/bible-navigator/real-presence/matthew2626-28)

- **Baptist/Evangelical Memorial View (Spurgeon, GTY):** The bread and cup are memorial symbols. Spurgeon says Christ "intended that broken bread to represent his body." The ordinance is done "in remembrance of Me" (Luke 22:19) — a mental act of remembering Christ's sacrifice, not a means of receiving His bodily presence. (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Guzik (Enduring Word) leans toward the memorial/symbolic view but emphasizes the practical point: "Beyond the debate over what the bread and the cup mean, we must remember what Jesus said to do with them. We must take and eat." The focus is on remembering Christ's broken body and shed blood. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/)

---

### v. 27 — "Then He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, 'Drink from it, all of you.'"

- **Traditional Reading (Ellicott, Gill, Enduring Word):** The better manuscripts omit the article — "a cup." In the Passover ritual, a cup of wine mingled with water was passed round three times. This was likely the third cup, called "the cup of blessing" (cf. 1 Cor. 10:16). Ellicott notes that one cup had already been passed earlier (Luke 22:17); now another becomes, "under a solemn consecration, the symbol of a diviner truth." The command "Drink from it, all of you" (Greek: *piete ex autou pantes*) emphasises that every disciple — not just the clergy — is to partake. Gill notes this refutes the Roman practice of withholding the cup from the laity. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm)

- **Catholic response (newadvent.org):** The Catholic Church teaches "concomitance" — since Christ is wholly present under either species (body, blood, soul, and divinity), receiving under one kind is receiving the whole Christ. The practice of communion under one kind developed for practical and reverential reasons, not as a denial of the laity's right. (newadvent.org/cathen/05572c.htm)

---

### v. 28 — "This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins."

- **Traditional Reading (Gill, Ellicott, Spurgeon, Enduring Word):** This is the institution of the **new covenant** (Jeremiah 31:31–34), sealed not with animal blood as the Sinai covenant was (Exodus 24:8), but with Christ's own blood. Gill notes that "poured out" (Greek: *ekchunnomenon*, present participle) indicates either the certainty of the imminent shedding, or that the blood is "in the act of being poured out." Only Matthew among the Synoptics adds "for the forgiveness of sins," directly connecting the Supper to the atoning purpose of Christ's death. **Spurgeon** exclaims: "In that large word 'many' let us exceedingly rejoice. Christ's blood was not shed for the handful of apostles alone." Enduring Word emphasises that "no mere man could ever institute a new covenant between God and man, but Jesus is the God-man." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm; preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/)

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** The Lord's Supper "signifies, seals, and exhibits to believing partakers the benefits of Christ's mediation." It is a "means of grace" — Christ is spiritually present and nourishes the souls of those who partake by faith. (learn.ligonier.org/articles/what-lords-supper)

- **Baptist (Desiring God):** The Table "serves as a means of Christ's ongoing grace to his church. Through the transpatial power of his Spirit, Jesus is spiritually present at the Table. We encounter him. He nourishes our souls." This is more than "mere memorialism" — there is a real spiritual feeding. (desiringgod.org/articles/what-is-the-lords-supper)

- **Catholic (Orchard's Catholic Commentary, StudyLight):** "The new covenant is now being liturgically concluded with the sacrificial blood of Christ." The Greek *ekchunnomenon* (present participle, possibly with future meaning) presents the blood "either in the state of being shed or as now dedicated to its shedding." The Apostles are to "make the sacrifice their own and thus achieve its purpose." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/matthew-26.html)

---

### v. 29 — "I tell you, I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father's kingdom."

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Enduring Word):** Spurgeon sees this as Jesus taking "the great Nazarite vow never to drink of the fruit of the vine till he should drink it new with his disciples in his Father's kingdom." Enduring Word notes this looks forward to "the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9)" — a future celebration in heaven. Jesus has not yet celebrated this with His people; He is waiting for all to be gathered. (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/)

- **Catholic (Orchard):** Placed by Luke 22:18 *before* the Institution, probably rightly, because the reflection belongs before the disciples' thoughts are raised to the Eucharistic cup. Matthew and Mark place it here because they are concerned only with "those elements of the Last Supper which were to endure." "This fruit of the vine" seems to refer to the unconsecrated cup from earlier in the meal. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/matthew-26.html)

---

### v. 30 — "And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives."

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Gill, Enduring Word):** The "hymn" was almost certainly the **Hallel** (Psalms 115–118), the traditional close of the Passover meal. Spurgeon marvels: "Was it not truly brave of our dear Lord to sing under such circumstances? He was going forth to his last dread conflict, to Gethsemane, and Gabbatha, and Golgotha; yet he went with a song on his lips. He must have led the singing, for the disciples were too sad to start the hallel." Gill adds that this was according to the Jewish custom of singing the "great Hallel" at the Passover. (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm)

---

### v. 31 — "Then Jesus said to them, 'This very night you will all fall away on account of Me. For it is written: "I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered."'"

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Enduring Word):** Jesus quotes **Zechariah 13:7**. Spurgeon highlights Jesus' habit of quoting Scripture even when speaking infallible truth: "He was able to speak words of infallible truth, yet he fell back upon the Inspired Record." The "Shepherd" is Jesus; the "sheep" are the disciples. The striking (by God's decree, through human instruments) and scattering would happen "this very night." Enduring Word notes the candor: Jesus didn't hide the hard truth from His disciples. (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/)

---

### v. 32 — "But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee."

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Enduring Word):** Spurgeon sees the Shepherd's care even after scattering: "the Shepherd would not lose them, there would be a reunion between him and his sheep." "I will go before you" suggests the Good Shepherd leading His flock after the Eastern manner. This promise would sustain them through the dark hours ahead. Enduring Word notes that Jesus predicted both the scattering and the regathering — the resurrection is central to His promise. (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/)

---

### vv. 33–35 — Peter's Protest and Jesus' Prediction of Denial

- **v. 33:** Spurgeon calls Peter's words "a very presumptuous speech" — not only self-confident but a "flat contradiction of the Master's declaration." Peter effectively says, "I know better than Christ." Yet Spurgeon grants Peter spoke from his heart, but "the heart is deceitful above all things."

- **v. 34:** Jesus specifies the denial will happen "this very night, before the rooster crows" — and that Peter will deny Him not once but "three times." Spurgeon: "Not only would he stumble and fall with his fellow-disciples, but he would go beyond them all." Gill explains that the cock-crowing marked the third watch of the night (the end of the night watch, near dawn), giving a specific time reference.

- **v. 35:** Peter doubles down, and "all the other disciples said the same thing." Spurgeon: "It was shameful that Peter should repeat his self-confident declaration in the teeth of Christ's express prediction concerning him." The other disciples join in — "They all felt that under no circumstances could they deny their Lord." (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm)

- **Baptist/Pentecostal application:** Enduring Word says Peter's overconfidence is a warning: self-reliance rather than dependence on Christ leads to spiritual failure. "Watch and pray" (v. 41) is the remedy. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/)

---

### v. 36 — "At that time Jesus went with His disciples to a place called Gethsemane, and He told them, 'Sit here while I go over there and pray.'"

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Gill, Enduring Word):** "Gethsemane" means "olive press" — a fitting name for the place where Jesus would be crushed under the weight of the world's sin. Spurgeon calls this "the Holy of Holies of our Lord's life on earth … a mystery like that which Moses saw when the bush burned with fire, and was not consumed." Jesus left eight disciples near the entrance while He went deeper. Gill notes this was Christ's customary place of retirement for prayer (John 18:2), which is why Judas knew where to find Him. (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm)

---

### vv. 37–38 — "He took with Him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee and began to be sorrowful and deeply distressed. Then He said to them, 'My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch with Me.'"

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Gill):** The three — Peter, James, and John — had witnessed His transfiguration; now they witness His agony. Spurgeon: "His sorrow was so great that he must bear it alone … 'I have trodden the winepress alone.'" "Sorrowful and deeply distressed" (Greek: *lupeisthai kai ademonein*) conveys overwhelming grief and anguish. "My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death" — Spurgeon says "the sorrow of his soul was the very soul of his sorrow … he seemed to reach the utmost limit of endurance." Gill explains this was not fear of death as such, but the bearing of the divine wrath against sin — the "soul-offering for sin." (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm)

---

### v. 39 — "Going a little farther, He fell facedown and prayed, 'My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.'"

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Gill, Enduring Word):** "Fell facedown" — the posture of utmost submission and desperation. The "cup" represents the full measure of divine wrath against sin that Jesus was about to drink. Gill: the prayer shows Christ's true humanity — He recoils from suffering, yet His will is perfectly submissive to the Father. Spurgeon emphasises "Yet not as I will, but as You will" as the supreme example of surrender. Enduring Word notes that Jesus' prayer wasn't a request to escape the cross altogether, but an honest cry from His humanity — yet always subordinate to the Father's will. The request "if it is possible" has been understood by many commentators as asking whether there was any other way to accomplish redemption. (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm)

---

### vv. 40–41 — "'Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?' He asked Peter. 'Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.'"

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Gill, Enduring Word):** Jesus returned to find the three sleeping. His question is directed to Peter — the one who had boasted loudest. Spurgeon observes: "They had never before seen their Lord overwhelmed with Atlantic billows of sorrow … yet they slept." "Watch and pray" is the antidote to Peter's self-confidence. Gill explains "the spirit is willing, but the body is weak" — even regenerate believers have a remaining corruption (the flesh) that wars against the renewed spirit. Enduring Word adds: the disciples' failure to watch and pray left them unprepared for the temptation that came when Jesus was arrested. (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/)

---

### v. 42 — "A second time He went away and prayed, 'My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, may Your will be done.'"

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Gill):** The second prayer shows a subtle shift — from "if it is possible, let this cup pass" to "if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it…" Gill sees this as Jesus' progressive acceptance, His human will being increasingly conformed to the divine will. Spurgeon says this is the only prayer of the three that Matthew records directly; the third (v. 44) merely says He "said the same thing." The repetition underscores the intensity of the struggle. (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm)

- **Precept Austin notes:** Matthew uniquely provides the second prayer as a direct quotation (one of the elements unique to Matthew's Passion narrative). (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary)

---

### vv. 43–44 — "And again Jesus returned and found them sleeping—for their eyes were heavy. So He left them and went away once more and prayed a third time, saying the same thing."

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Gill):** "Their eyes were heavy" — Gill attributes this partly to natural fatigue (it was late at night after a full meal) and partly to the grief that had overcome them (Luke 22:45 says they were "sleeping from sorrow"). Spurgeon is gentler than some commentators, noting that sorrow itself can produce exhaustion. The threefold prayer parallels the threefold denial to come — and perhaps Paul's threefold plea regarding the thorn (2 Cor. 12:8). (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm)

---

### vv. 45–46 — "'Are you still sleeping and resting? Look, the hour is near, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go! See, My betrayer is approaching!'"

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Gill):** Spurgeon does *not* think Jesus was being ironic: "I do not think Jesus was speaking ironically when he said, 'Sleep on now, and take your rest' — but that he allowed them to take a little sleep while he sat by, and watched." He suggests the Lord sat watching over them briefly before the arrest. "Not long did he sit, or did they sleep; for through the olives he could see the glare of the approaching torches." Gill takes a different view: he reads it as a sharp rebuke — "Are you still sleeping?" — meaning, "Is this a time for sleep?" "Rise, let us go!" — Jesus goes not to flee but to meet His betrayer. Enduring Word: Jesus had won the battle in prayer and now moves forward with calm resolution. (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/)

---

### v. 47 — "While Jesus was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, accompanied by a large crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests and elders of the people."

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Gill, Enduring Word):** The timing underscores Jesus' control — "while He was still speaking." Judas came with "a great multitude" — likely a cohort of Roman soldiers (John 18:3 mentions a *speira*, a cohort of up to 600 men) plus temple guards. Gill notes the irony that they came armed as if to capture a dangerous criminal, when Jesus had taught openly in the temple daily. Enduring Word: "They clearly regarded Jesus as a dangerous man." Spurgeon: "It is a remarkable fact that we do not read, in the New Testament, that any one of the twelve, except Judas, ever kissed Jesus. It seems as if the most impudent familiarity was very near akin to dastardly treachery." (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/)

---

### vv. 48–49 — "Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them: 'The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him.' Going directly to Jesus, he said, 'Greetings, Rabbi!' and kissed Him."

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Ellicott, Gill):** The kiss was the customary greeting of a disciple to a rabbi — which made it the height of hypocrisy. Ellicott notes the Greek word for "kissed" (*katephilesen*) carries the sense of kissing fervently or affectionately (the same word used of the woman who kissed Jesus' feet in Luke 7). Spurgeon: "Judas said, 'Hail, master' and kissed him much (R.V. margin); betraying him by the act that ought to have been the token of firmest friendship." Gill notes that the "sign" was necessary because in the darkness of the garden, the soldiers could not distinguish Jesus from the others. Spurgeon adds a striking observation: "This sign of Judas was typical of the way in which Jesus is generally betrayed! When men intend to undermine the inspiration of the Scriptures, how do they begin their books? Why, always with a declaration that they wish to promote the truth of Christ!" (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm)

---

### v. 50 — "'Friend,' Jesus replied, 'do what you came for.' Then the men stepped forward, seized Jesus, and arrested Him."

- **Traditional Reading (Spurgeon, Ellicott, Gill):** The word "Friend" (Greek: *hetairos*) is not the warm "beloved friend" (*philos*) but "comrade" or "mate" — a term used between fellow-soldiers or companions. Ellicott notes Socrates used it with his students. Spurgeon marvels: "The meek and lowly Jesus spake not as any mere man might have done under such circumstances. He did not address Judas as, 'Wretch!' or, 'Miscreant!' but his first word, after receiving the traitor's kiss, was, 'Friend!'" Gill understands the phrase as "do that for which thou art come" — Jesus knows exactly what Judas intends and permits it. The BSB renders it "do what you came for." Enduring Word notes the contrast between Judas' hollow "Greetings, Rabbi!" and Jesus' still-loving "Friend." (preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/)

- **Catholic Commentary (Orchard):** Notes that this is one of the elements unique to Matthew's account in the Passion narrative — Jesus' words to Judas after the kiss. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/matthew-26.html)

## Summary of Traditions Where They Differ

| Issue | Reformed/Presbyterian | Lutheran | Baptist (Spurgeon/GTY) | Pentecostal (Enduring Word) | Catholic |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Christ's presence in Supper | Real spiritual presence; Christ received by faith | Real bodily presence "in, with, and under" elements | Memorial/symbolic; spiritual nourishment by faith | Symbolic/memorial emphasis; focus on "take and eat" | Transubstantiation — bread and wine become actual Body and Blood |
| Cup for laity | All partake | All partake | All partake | All partake | Concomitance — receiving under one kind sufficient |
| The Supper as sacrifice | Commemorative; no re-sacrifice | Commemorative | Commemorative | Commemorative | Unbloody re-presentation of Christ's sacrifice |
